set.statement: In adults aged 18 or older living in US households and some group homes, a national face-to-face survey in 2012–2013 (NESARC-III; 36,309 people, 60.1% response; Grant et al., 2015; funded by the US National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism, which also ran the survey, and the National Institute on Drug Abuse; no conflicts declared) found DSM-5 alcohol use disorder, diagnosed with a structured interview (the AUDADIS-5) given by interviewers who were not clinicians, in 13.9 in 100 adults in the past year (SE 0.31) and in 29.1 in 100 at some time in their lives. About half of the past-year cases were mild (7.3 in 100 adults mild, 3.2 moderate, 3.4 severe). The disorder was more common in men than in women (17.6 against 10.4 in 100 in the past year) and at ages 18 to 29 (26.7 in 100) than at 65 or older (2.3 in 100). Among adults who had drunk alcohol in the past year, 17.5 in 100 (95% CI 16.7 to 18.3) met the older DSM-IV criteria in the same survey, as did 54.5 in 100 of those who had drunk heavily at least once a week (4 or more US standard drinks of 14 g of alcohol in a day for women, 5 or more for men) (Grant et al., 2017). The figures depend on the survey: another national survey, cited by the same authors, found 7.0 in 100 adults with the disorder in the past year in 2013 and about 7.5 in 100 throughout 2002 to 2013, a little over half of NESARC-III's 12.7 in 100 by the older DSM-IV definition, against which the authors set it; they do not explain the difference. NESARC-III left out homeless people, people in prison and most people in treatment, which the authors say may lower its figures, and 4 in 10 of the people sampled did not take part. By the older DSM-IV definition, the same institute's surveys found 8.5 in 100 adults with the disorder in 2001–2002 and 12.7 in 100 in 2012–2013. The authors read this as a real rise, pointing to near-identical questions, weighting for non-response and other alcohol indicators that rose over the same years (Grant et al., 2017); in the editors' reading these surveys cannot show whether the disorder became more common, because their design and response differed (81.0% against about 60%) and the other national survey, as the authors report it, showed a stable figure over the same years. For the world, a narrative review relays WHO estimates for 2016 of 5.1 in 100 people aged 15 or older (8.6 in 100 men, 1.7 in 100 women), which its authors call rough estimates; these figures are second-hand (Carvalho et al., 2019). Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
set.plain: In a large US survey in 2012–2013, about 14 in 100 adults had alcohol use disorder in the past year, about half of them in a mild form, and about 29 in 100 had had it at some time in their lives. It was most common in young adults and in men. Among adults who drank that year, about 18 in 100 met the older (DSM-IV) criteria. Another US survey found a little over half as many people with the disorder, so the number depends on how it is measured, and the survey left out people who were homeless or in prison and most people in treatment. A review passes on world estimates of about 5 in 100 people aged 15 or older in 2016. The survey's authors think the disorder became more common in the US between 2001 and 2013; in our reading, their two surveys were run too differently to show that.
set.grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: Study card sc_grant_2015 (JBI prevalence checklist), overall moderate: 60.1% response managed by weighting on a few characteristics; a household frame that leaves out homeless, imprisoned and most treated people, which the authors say biases the figure down; diagnosis by interviewers who were not clinicians (stated in Grant et al., 2017), with fair-to-good agreement with clinicians (kappa 0.49 to 0.62). The change between the 2001–2002 and 2012–2013 surveys is rated high risk of bias on sc_grant_2017, which is why no trend is claimed.
set.grade.domains.inconsistency.note: Another national survey, as the same authors report it, gives a little over half the past-year figure (7.0% in 2013 and about 7.5% throughout 2002–2013, against 12.7% by DSM-IV and 13.9% by DSM-5 in NESARC-III); the surveys differ in instrument, sponsor and design, and the authors call for research on the discrepancy. The other survey was not read; its figures are taken as the authors give them, and the stable 2002–2013 figure is cited in the paper to a 2004 NESARC article that cannot contain it (reporting issue on sc_grant_2015).
set.grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim (prevalence in survey populations): it starts low and is never upgraded. Rated down one level for risk of bias (response, frame and diagnosis by interviewers who were not clinicians; JBI moderate on the card) and one for inconsistency (another national survey gives a little over half the past-year figure, unexplained), which reaches very low. The prevalence among people who drink (Grant et al., 2017) comes from the same 2012–2013 survey and is not independent of Grant et al. (2015). The rise from 2001–2002 to 2012–2013 is reported with the authors' reading (a real rise, supported in their view by near-identical questions, non-response weighting and other alcohol indicators) and with the editors' reasons why it cannot be read as a change in the population (sc_grant_2017: risk of bias high for the change; response 81.0% against about 60%; the other survey stable). The world figure comes from a narrative review relaying WHO (Carvalho et al., 2019), is second-hand and is not graded here. Status mixed: two US national surveys give inconsistent past-year figures, and no adequate explanation is offered.

set.plain: In a US survey in 2012–2013, about 20 in 100 people who had ever had alcohol use disorder said they had ever looked for treatment or help, and about 8 in 100 of those who had it in the past year. Groups such as Alcoholics Anonymous were the most common kind of help. People who had ever had severe disorder looked for help more often (about 35 in 100) than people with mild disorder (about 4 in 100). A review passes on figures of about 22 in 100 for Europe and the world, though these count people who received treatment, not people who looked for it. People reported this themselves, and the survey did not include most people who were in treatment at the time.

set.plain: Delirium tremens, or the DTs, is sudden confusion during alcohol withdrawal: trouble paying attention and thinking clearly that comes and goes, together with withdrawal signs such as shaking or a fast pulse. A review says it usually starts about 3 days after withdrawal begins and lasts 2 or 3 days, that 3 to 5 in 100 people in hospital for withdrawal get it, and that about 1 to 4 in 100 hospital patients with the DTs die. In old trials, about 6 in 100 people in withdrawal who were given dummy pills developed delirium; most of these people were in one large trial from 1969. The review names recent seizures, earlier DTs, older age and other illnesses as signs that it is more likely. These figures are old or passed on by one review, and none measures how often it happens outside hospital.
set.grade.domains.indirectness.note: The placebo groups are from trials of 1961 to 1980, before DSM-IV; the review says their outcomes corresponded to DSM-IV definitions but not how this was judged, and their settings are not described; the relayed figures concern hospital patients; no source measures delirium in people stopping outside hospital.

set.statement: In adults with alcohol dependence treated as outpatients in double-blind trials, mostly after detoxification and with counselling or another psychosocial treatment in both groups, naltrexone tablets at the dose used in most trials compared with placebo reduced return to heavy drinking (in most trials 5 or more drinks in a day for men, 4 or more for women) during treatment: across 19 trials of 12 to 24 weeks (17 of them of 12 weeks) pooled in a review for the US Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, 728 of 1,593 people on naltrexone (46 in 100) and 698 of 1,282 on placebo (54 in 100) returned to heavy drinking (crude totals, editors' arithmetic), a pooled difference of 9 in 100 (risk difference −0.09, 95% CI −0.13 to −0.04; 12 people treated for one to benefit) (Jonas et al., 2014; funded by the agency; no conflicts declared). Its 2023 update, also for the agency (no conflicts declared), found a risk ratio of 0.81 (0.72 to 0.90; 23 trials, 3,170 people) (McPheeters et al., 2023), and a Cochrane review of naltrexone in any form, mostly the same tablets, found 0.83 (0.76 to 0.90; 28 trials, 4,433 people) (Rösner et al., 2010; funded by the German education and research ministry; two of its six authors declare fees from drug companies). The effect on staying off alcohol completely was small or unclear: risk difference −0.05 (−0.10 to −0.002) in 2014, risk ratio 0.93 (0.87 to 0.99) in 2023 and 0.96 (0.92 to 1.00) in the Cochrane review. In the 2023 review, people on naltrexone drank on about 5 fewer days in every 100 (−5.1 percentage points, −7.16 to −3.04) and drank heavily on about 4 fewer (−4.3, −7.60 to −0.91). With naltrexone at any dose (the 2023 review assessed harms for all doses together), nausea (risk ratio 1.73, 1.51 to 1.98), dizziness (1.99, 1.47 to 2.69) and vomiting (1.53, 1.23 to 1.91) were more common; about 1 more person in 48 stopped a trial because of side effects (number needed to harm 48, 30 to 112), and serious adverse events were not more frequent (risk difference −0.02, −0.05 to 0.00; 9 trials). A higher oral dose and a long-acting injection were each tested in only 2 trials for return to heavy drinking, without a clear effect. Head to head, naltrexone and acamprosate did not differ (return to heavy drinking risk ratio 1.02, 0.93 to 1.11; 4 trials), but more than half of the people in this comparison were in one US trial (COMBINE, 612 of 1,141, editors' arithmetic), whose naltrexone group took the higher oral dose. Evidence on deaths, injuries and quality of life is insufficient. The three reviews share most of their trials and are one body of evidence, not three. Across the 2023 review's trials of all medicines, mean age was typically 40 to 49 and most trials that reported race and sex enrolled mostly White men; most participants had moderate to severe dependence and had stopped drinking before starting, and effects in people still drinking, with mild disorder or without counselling are uncertain. Certainty: moderate. Status: replicated.
set.plain: In trials lasting mostly 3 months, people with alcohol dependence who took naltrexone tablets went back to heavy drinking less often than people on dummy pills: about 46 in 100 against 54 in 100. Naltrexone helped less, if at all, with stopping drinking completely. People on it drank on about 5 fewer days in every 100. Feeling sick, dizziness and vomiting were more common, and about 1 more person in 48 stopped because of side effects. Naltrexone and acamprosate did about the same when compared directly, though most people in that comparison were in one trial. Most people in the trials were middle-aged men who had already stopped drinking and also had counselling.
set.grade.reasoning: Randomized trials start high; rated down one level for risk of bias, giving moderate, as both AHRQ reviews graded return to heavy drinking. 'Reduces' applies to return to heavy drinking; the effect on any drinking is small and depends on the review and model (significant in 2014 and 2023, not in the Cochrane random-effects model), and the claim says so. The duration is given as in the pooled trials (12 to 24 weeks, mostly 12, in the 2014 pools), not as the 12 to 52 weeks of all the review's studies. Overlap: the 2023 review updates the 2014 one (81 of its 118 trials carried over), the Cochrane review covers largely the same trials to January 2010, and COMBINE is in all three, so they are counted as one body of evidence; COMBINE also supplies more than half of the head-to-head comparison with acamprosate, with its higher-dose naltrexone group. Status replicated: that body holds many independent trials pointing the same way. The higher oral dose and the injection are named only as tested in 2 trials each for return to heavy drinking; no doses are given.
set.grade.domains.indirectness.note: Worded for the trial populations (detoxified, mostly treatment-seeking adults with moderate to severe dependence, with counselling) and durations (mostly 12 weeks in the main 2014 pools); the uncertainty outside them is stated.

set.statement: In people with alcohol dependence, mostly adults treated as outpatients, in double-blind trials, most of them European and most after detoxification, acamprosate compared with placebo is associated with fewer people returning to any drinking during treatment: across 16 trials pooled in a review for the US Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, 1,968 of 2,576 people on acamprosate (76 in 100) and 1,893 of 2,271 on placebo (83 in 100) drank again (crude totals and a crude difference of 7 in 100, editors' arithmetic), a pooled difference of 9 in 100 (risk difference −0.09, 95% CI −0.14 to −0.04; 12 people treated for one to benefit), with large differences between trials (I² 80.8%) (Jonas et al., 2014; funded by the agency; no conflicts declared); its 2023 update, also for the agency, gives a risk ratio of 0.88 (0.83 to 0.93; 20 trials, 6,380 people) (McPheeters et al., 2023), and a Cochrane review 0.86 (0.81 to 0.91; 24 trials) (Rösner et al., 2010; funded by the German education and research ministry, with individual patient data from a database part-funded by the manufacturer; three of its six authors declare fees from drug companies, two of them from makers or marketers of acamprosate). In the Cochrane review abstinent days rose by about 11 in every 100 days (10.94 percentage points, 5.08 to 16.81; I² 94%), and in 7 trials fewer people on acamprosate had returned to drinking 3 to 12 months after treatment ended (risk ratio 0.91, 0.87 to 0.96). Acamprosate did not reduce return to heavy drinking (risk ratio 0.99, 0.94 to 1.05; 7 trials). In the 4 trials at low risk of bias the difference was not clear (risk difference −0.02, −0.09 to 0.05); the two of them with by far the most events, both in the US and one of them COMBINE, found no benefit, while most of the other 15 trials were European and recruited from inpatient settings or treatment programmes. The 2014 authors list population differences, other heterogeneity, chance or 'no true association between acamprosate and return to drinking' as possible explanations. Of the Cochrane review's 24 trials, 17 were run or supported by drug companies, mostly the manufacturer, though industry-run and non-profit trials gave similar estimates (risk ratios 0.88 and 0.88). Diarrhoea was more common (11 more in 100; risk difference 0.11, 0.09 to 0.13), and in the 2014 review so were anxiety (2 trials) and vomiting (4 trials); more people stopped because of side effects in the Cochrane review (risk ratio 1.35, 1.01 to 1.80), but not significantly more in the 2014 review. Head to head, acamprosate and naltrexone did not differ (return to any drinking risk ratio 1.03, 0.96 to 1.10; 3 trials, 612 of whose 800 people were in COMBINE, whose naltrexone group took the higher oral dose; editors' arithmetic). The three reviews share most of their trials. Certainty: low. Status: mixed.
set.plain: In trials, mostly in Europe, fewer people with alcohol dependence who took acamprosate drank again during treatment than people on dummy pills: about 76 in 100 against 83 in 100. It did not cut heavy drinking. The most carefully run trials, including the two largest of them, both in the US, found no clear difference, and most trials were run or supported by drug companies, mostly its maker. Diarrhoea was more common: about 11 more people in every 100. In one review, more people stopped taking it because of side effects. Acamprosate and naltrexone did about the same when compared directly.

set.statement: In adults with alcohol use disorder in double-blind outpatient trials of at least 12 weeks, mostly with a psychosocial co-intervention, other medicines compared with placebo, as pooled in a 2023 review for the US Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (McPheeters et al., 2023; funded by the agency; no conflicts declared): topiramate is associated with fewer drinking days (−7.2 percentage points, 95% CI −14.3 to −0.1; 8 trials, 1,080 people), fewer heavy-drinking days (−6.2, −10.9 to −1.4; 9 trials) and about 2 fewer drinks on drinking days (−2.0, −3.1 to −1.0; 7 trials), each graded moderate strength of evidence by the review, with more tingling (risk ratio 3.08, 2.11 to 4.49), changes in taste (3.01, 1.70 to 5.34) and problems with thinking (2.37, 1.58 to 3.55); baclofen with fewer people returning to any drinking (risk ratio 0.83, 0.70 to 0.98; 8 trials), though not with its other drinking outcomes, and gabapentin with fewer returning to heavy drinking (0.90, 0.82 to 0.98; 3 trials), both graded low, with more drowsiness, sleepiness or dizziness and, with gabapentin, problems with thinking (2.76, 1.51 to 5.06). Disulfiram showed no clear difference in return to any drinking in blinded trials (risk ratio 1.03, 0.90 to 1.17; 3 trials; low), although no trial tested taking it under supervision, which the earlier review says may underestimate its benefit (Jonas et al., 2014). A long-acting injection of naltrexone showed no clear difference in return to any or heavy drinking (2 trials each; low) but was linked to fewer heavy-drinking days (−4.68 percentage points, −8.63 to −0.73; 3 trials; low). In the earlier review, nalmefene was associated with 2 fewer heavy-drinking days a month (−2.0, −3.0 to −1.0; 2 trials), and about 1 more person in 12 stopped a trial because of side effects (number needed to harm 12, 7 to 50). Deaths were too few to judge (8 with baclofen against 3 with placebo in 4 trials). The 2023 review updates the 2014 one and shares most of its trials, and it reports results only for medicines with at least low strength of evidence for benefit. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
set.plain: Several other medicines have been compared with dummy pills. Topiramate was linked to fewer drinking days (about 7 fewer in every 100) and about 2 fewer drinks on drinking days, but tingling, changes in taste and trouble thinking were more common. Baclofen and gabapentin were linked to small benefits, but the evidence is weak. In blinded trials, disulfiram showed no clear benefit; no trial tested taking it with someone watching. A long-acting naltrexone injection showed no clear effect on going back to drinking, though it was linked to fewer heavy-drinking days. Most of these medicines were tested in only a few trials.

set.statement: In adults with alcohol dependence at 11 US academic centres who had stopped drinking 4 to 21 days earlier (COMBINE, 1,383 people randomized, 2001 to 2004; Anton et al., 2006; funded by the US National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism, with medicines and placebos donated by Lipha Pharmaceuticals, a maker of acamprosate, and several authors reporting fees or grants from drug companies), adding up to 20 sessions of a specialist talking therapy (combined behavioural intervention) to medicine and nine medical-support visits did not detectably improve drinking during 16 weeks of treatment, while with placebo pills the therapy was linked to more days without alcohol. With naltrexone, the combination was no better than either alone: abstinent days were 77.1 in 100 with naltrexone and the therapy, 80.6 with naltrexone alone, 79.2 with the therapy and placebo naltrexone and 75.1 with placebo naltrexone alone (each group pooled over acamprosate or its placebo; naltrexone × therapy interaction P = 0.009), and only naltrexone alone differed clearly from placebo naltrexone alone (Cohen d 0.22, 97.5% CI 0.03 to 0.40; therapy with placebo 0.17, −0.02 to 0.35; both 0.07, −0.11 to 0.25). Averaged over all the pill groups, abstinent days were 78.2 against 77.8 in 100 (d 0.01, −0.12 to 0.14), an interval that excludes more than a small gain, and the chance of a first heavy-drinking day was not clearly lower (hazard ratio 0.81, 0.60 to 1.10, the paper's main-effect estimate, which by its interval may compare only two single groups), an interval that does not rule out a sizeable benefit; the authors say these averages must be read with caution because of the interaction. Among people given only placebo pills and medical support, those who also had the therapy had more abstinent days (79.8 against 73.8 in 100; P = 0.04 in a corrected post hoc comparison), and the authors read the results as the therapy helping when naltrexone was not given. More people had a good overall outcome at the end of treatment with naltrexone (74 in 100), the therapy (71) or both (74) than with placebo pills and medical support alone (58), a secondary outcome with more missing data than the main ones. People given the therapy without pills or medical management had fewer abstinent days (66.6 in 100) than either group on placebo pills and medical support. In the year after treatment the pattern changed: the combination no longer lagged (interaction P = 0.27; abstinent days 61.4 in 100 with placebo naltrexone alone, 66.2 with naltrexone, 66.6 with the therapy and 67.3 with both), and none of the differences was clear (the therapy averaged over the pill groups 66.9 against 63.8, P = 0.08). The trial had low power for combinations (0.40 to 0.50), the therapy could not be hidden from participants, drinking was self-reported to staff who knew who had the therapy, and people needing psychiatric medicines or with other recent drug use disorders (except nicotine or cannabis) were left out. In most other trials of medicines both groups received some psychosocial treatment, so those trials show what medicines add to it (Jonas et al., 2014). Certainty: low. Status: single study.
set.plain: In one large US trial, adults with alcohol dependence who took naltrexone and had nine short check-ins with a health worker did as well as those who also had up to 20 sessions of specialist talking therapy: combining the two added nothing. For people on dummy pills, adding the therapy was linked to more days without alcohol in one comparison. On an overall measure of doing well, naltrexone, the therapy or both were each better than dummy pills alone. People who had the therapy without pills or the medicine check-ins had fewer days without alcohol. In the year after treatment, no difference between the groups was clear. The trial was not built to test combinations, and drinking was reported by the people themselves.
set.grade.reasoning: A randomized trial starts high; rated down for risk of bias (unblinded therapy with self-reported outcomes) and imprecision (low power for combinations), giving low. 'Does not detectably change' concerns adding the therapy to medicine: with naltrexone the combination was no better than naltrexone alone, and the main effect on abstinent days averaged over the pill groups has an interval that excludes more than a small gain (d up to 0.14), though the authors caution that the averages are hard to read given the interaction. With placebo pills the therapy was linked to more abstinent days (d 0.17, −0.02 to 0.35, in the factorial comparison; P = .04 in a corrected post hoc comparison of the two groups given only placebo pills), which the statement reports. The heavy-drinking interval does not rule out a benefit, and the trial was not powered for combinations. Status single study. The other trials of medicines (Jonas et al., 2014) give both groups psychosocial treatment, so they do not test whether therapy adds to medicine and are cited only to frame what their estimates mean.

set.plain: In 1973, a team in Seattle described eight young children, five girls and three boys, born to mothers who had had alcoholism for years and drank heavily all through pregnancy. All eight were small before and after birth and did not catch up, had short eye openings and were behind in development; seven had small heads, and many had a small upper jaw, unusual palm creases, joint problems or heart problems. The paper did not yet use the name fetal alcohol syndrome. It describes selected children: some were chosen because they had these signs, milder cases were left out, there was no comparison group, and the amount of drinking was not recorded. Four of the six mothers with a record lost weight during pregnancy, and the study could not separate nutrition from alcohol. So it cannot show how often these signs follow heavy drinking in pregnancy, or what caused them.
